You are a scientific evidence extractor. Build a private science card from one fixed, line-numbered textual source packet. You are not authoring a benchmark case.
Return exactly one JSON object matching the supplied schema, without Markdown or extra text.
Use only the supplied source. Do not use outside knowledge or infer missing facts from citations.
Copy the supplied citation, canonical journal DOI, and versioned arXiv ID exactly.
Except for mechanism.variable_names, names and IDs must be ASCII snake-style identifiers. Source-significant uppercase segments such as E_i or T_low may be retained; the next deterministic stage lowercases them for runtime use. mechanism.variable_names may preserve arbitrary raw paper notation.
Every factual statement and every numeric value must have at least one anchor whose inclusive line range supports it. Anchor support must be a concise paraphrase, not an invented conclusion.
Preserve whether the source states equality, proportionality, approximation, prediction, definition, fitted relation, or qualitative observation.
Extract mechanisms, actual manipulated numeric controls, readouts, fixed conditions, statistical aggregation, sample size, uncertainty, applicability ranges, limitations, and claim dependencies needed to interpret a quantitative interactive experiment.
A control is a numeric quantity the study actually manipulates. A readout is a measured or computed observable. Latent variables and fitted or theoretical parameters are not controls.
Sample size, ensemble count, averaging rule, fit method, and uncertainty convention are statistical provenance, not physical fixed conditions and never a hidden-world discriminator. Record them in ScienceReadout.statistic/uncertainty and claim.statistical_basis/uncertainty instead of fixed_conditions. These fields describe the source data; they will not be copied onto a deterministic Oracle query.
Represent source support without inventing continuity: use domain_kind continuous_interval only for a source-supported nonzero interval, numeric_values for explicitly reported discrete manipulated settings, fixed_value for one setting, symbolic for a stated nonnumeric domain, and unreported when the source does not provide one. Only continuous_interval and numeric_values can later compile to Player controls. A fixed value belongs to the experimental context, not a range with equal endpoints. The quantity that distinguishes the two selected source-reported branches is private regime context, not a Player control: represent each branch value or limit as its own branch-specific fixed condition, and make the corresponding claim cite only its branch condition. Two isolated reported condition values do not license interpolation. Never borrow a numeric domain from one claim for another claim merely because they use the same symbol.
Use this exact domain-field table for every control and claim domain: continuous_interval => numeric minimum, numeric maximum with minimum < maximum, allowed_values=[]; numeric_values => minimum=null, maximum=null, at least two unique allowed_values; fixed_value => minimum=null, maximum=null, exactly one allowed_value; symbolic or unreported => minimum=null, maximum=null, allowed_values=[], and a non-empty domain_statement. A one-sided or otherwise non-numeric source condition is not a continuous_interval with a null endpoint. When a reviewer figure-evidence addendum conservatively identifies a finite query set but not a continuous source interval, encode those supported values as numeric_values.
For every quantitative response that could become an Oracle equation, record each fitted coefficient and exponent as a named ScienceParameter under its linked mechanism. The parameter value is the central value; put the paper's uncertainty text in uncertainty. Never leave a numeric coefficient or exponent only inside claim.quantitative_form. If the meaning of a reported plus/minus value is not specified, write source_unspecified; do not guess standard error or confidence interval.
For every retained claim, encode the central-value control-to-readout relation in claim.oracle_outputs using the supplied expression AST. Output keys must exactly equal that claim's readout_names. A {"var": ...} leaf must name one of that claim's control_names. A {"param": ...} leaf must name a ScienceParameter belonging to one of that claim's mechanism_ids. Every scientific constant, including zero or one when it occurs in the source equation, must be a named, anchored ScienceParameter referenced by a param leaf. Numeric literals are forbidden in ScienceClaim oracle_outputs; structural selector literals are added only by the deterministic case binder. Keep quantitative_form as a human-readable rendering of the same relation. Do not put uncertainty ranges into oracle_outputs: the executable Oracle evaluates only source-reported central parameter values. Keep source aggregation, data-point error bars, fit-parameter uncertainty, and their conventions in the provenance fields; they are not uncertainty on each deterministic query result.
An unspecified plus/minus convention is missing metadata, not a contradiction: do not create a source_ambiguity solely because the paper omits whether a quoted fit uncertainty is a standard error, confidence interval, or another convention. Preserve the numeric plus/minus values in the quantitative form and parameter records, mark their meaning source_unspecified, and keep point error bars such as one standard deviation separate when the source defines them.
Parameter names must be globally unique, including after lowercasing. Qualify names by readout and regime when the paper reports several amplitudes, exponents, or other quantities of the same kind.
Keep variable_names in the paper's recognizable notation when useful (for example tau_Q); unlike executable parameter names, they need not be lower_snake_case.
Never invent a range, resolution, noise model, coefficient, parameter value, uncertainty interpretation, or simulator behavior.
Keep general mechanisms and linked empirical claims together rather than atomizing every equation into an unrelated mini-case. claim.mechanism_ids cites mechanisms. claim.depends_on may cite only other claim_ids, never mechanism_ids; use an empty array when a claim has no claim-level prerequisite.
Extract only the single best complete quantitative cluster for this authoring run; do not catalogue a second, unrelated experiment. Prefer two source-reported regimes that can use the same one-to-five controls and one-or-two readouts. If no such pair exists, extract the best single response faithfully and set case_authoring_ready false. Include every fixed condition, statistic, uncertainty, applicability limit, and branch parameter needed to reproduce the selected responses. Every quantitative claim must cite every selected mechanism that supplies a coefficient, exponent, or equation used by that claim. If the same paper symbol has a different meaning or source-supported domain in another experiment, omit that other experiment rather than merging or widening the selected control. Do not exhaust the output budget cataloguing unrelated qualitative results.
Do not bundle a condition that changes between reported regimes into a common fixed condition. Split the common apparatus settings from each regime-specific value, and link each claim only to compatible conditions.
Include only fixed conditions needed to interpret the selected discovery formula. Omit global simulation or acquisition settings that do not enter the selected response, especially when their locator contains a branch-specific value incompatible with the other branch.
Preserve operational definitions separately from captions and fitted relations. A readout anchor must cover how the observable is defined; claim anchors must additionally cover the equation, domain, aggregation, and uncertainty convention they assert. For each claim, control_domains must give one separately anchored source-applicability domain for every cited control, preserving whether it is an interval, discrete values, fixed value, symbolic statement, or unreported; never substitute the broader paper-level control domain. For each readout, resolution is either a separately anchored measurement_resolution/reporting_increment object or null when the source supports neither. Do not infer resolution from uncertainty or silently treat decimal formatting as instrument resolution.
When the paper overloads notation or distinguishes a crossing-relative quantity from an absolute one, create separate readouts or claims and record the ambiguity. Never combine their equations or speculate why one presentation differs.
When main text, caption, appendix, or supplement uses materially different definitions or formulas, record the issue in source_ambiguities and do not silently reconcile it. Link every ambiguity to all affected claims, mechanisms, controls, readouts, and fixed conditions; leave all reference arrays empty only when the ambiguity affects the paper globally.
Set case_authoring_ready true only when the extracted evidence can support at least one numeric control, one numeric readout, one quantitative mechanism, and an objective source-grounded response within an explicit domain.
Do not generate Player background, initial observations, episode budgets, diagnostic or hidden conditions, counterfactuals, or code. The claim.oracle_outputs source relation is the only expression tree requested at this extraction stage.

L000046	\begin{abstract}
L000047	We present a closed-form expression for the contribution of surface defects to the supersymmetric Rényi entropy in six-dimensional $(2,0)$ theories. L000052	\textit{Introduction.}
L000053	Defects play a pivotal role in quantum field theory, with familiar examples including Wilson lines and Wilson surfaces. These defects often represent external probes coupled to the theory, such as a charged heavy probe particle in gauge theory, which is described by a Wilson line and serves as a key tool for understanding the non-perturbative properties of the theory. Meanwhile, entanglement entropy (EE) and R\'enyi entropy have garnered significant attention in recent years for their role in linking information theory, field theory, and gravity. These quantities are closely related to conformal anomalies in conformal field theories and can be computed holographically. As a one-parameter generalization of EE, R\'enyi entropy provides deeper insights into the structure of quantum field theories, making it essential to account for defect contributions to R\'enyi entropy.
L000054	
L000055	While the defect contribution to EE has been studied in previous works~\cite{Jensen:2013lxa,Lewkowycz:2013laa,Kobayashi:2018lil,Estes:2018tnu,Gentle:2015jma,Gentle:2015ruo}, a method for computing the corresponding contributions to R\'enyi entropy has remained elusive. In this letter, we take a significant step forward by calculating the contribution of surface defects to the supersymmetric R\'enyi entropy. A key motivation for studying surface defects in six dimensions is to gain insights into $(2,0)$ theories, whose proper formulation remains a challenging open problem. By combining supersymmetry with R\'enyi entropy, one can define a supersymmetric refinement of the ordinary R\'enyi entropy for these theories, as proposed in prior works~\cite{Nian:2015xky,Zhou:2015kaj}. This approach involves placing $(2,0)$ theories on $\mathbb{S}^1_\beta \times \mathbb{H}^5$ with an additional R-symmetry background field. Notably, the supersymmetric R\'enyi entropy exhibits universal relations with the conformal and 't Hooft anomalies and can be computed holographically via two-charge hyperbolic black holes in the large $N$ limit.
L000056	
L000057	Building on these developments, we analyze the contribution of the most natural operator, the surface operator, in $(2,0)$ theories on $\mathbb{S}^1_\beta \times \mathbb{H}^5$. Our findings reveal that the surface operator contribution to the supersymmetric R\'enyi entropy is a linear function of $1/n$ and directly proportional to $2b - d_2$, where $b$ and $d_2$ are the Weyl anomaly coefficients associated with the surface defect. Additionally, we derive a closed-form expression for the defect contribution to the supersymmetric Casimir energy, which simplifies to $-d_2$ (up to a proportionality constant) in the chiral algebra limit.

L000060	\textit{Defects in CFTs.} Starting with a $d$-dimensional Euclidean CFT in flat space $\mathbb{R}^d$, introducing a $p$-dimensional planar conformal defect will break its conformal symmetry $SO(1, d + 1)$ to $SO(1, p + 1) \times SO(d - p)$. The CFT stress-energy tensor one-point function $\langle T_{\mu\nu} \rangle$ in flat space vanishes due to the conformal symmetry. However, in the presence of defect, this one-point function does not necessarily vanish. If the planar defect is located at $x^i=0$, we can write the ambient metric as $\text{d}s^2 = \text{d} \hat x^a \text{d} \hat x^a + \text{d}x^i \text{d}x^i$, with $a=0, \dots, p-1$ the indices labeling the directions parallel to the defect and $i=p, \dots, d-1$ for the transverse directions. Varying the defect partition function gives the defect CFT stress-energy tensor, which can be split into the ambient part $T^{\mu\nu}$ and the defect localized part $\hat{T}^{ab}$~\cite{Billo:2016cpy,Kobayashi:2018lil}. The ambient stress-energy tensor is a symmetric traceless tensor of dimension $d$ and spin $2$, and from the (partial) conservation and residual conformal symmetry, its one-point function in the presence of the defect can be fixed~\footnote{The notation $\llangle O \rrangle$ refers to the correlation function measured in the presence of defect $\llangle O \rrangle \equiv \langle O D \rangle / \langle D \rangle$, where $D$ denotes the defect. }
L000061	\begin{equation}\label{Tbulk}
L000062	\begin{split}
L000063	\llangle T^{ab} \rrangle &= -\frac{d - p - 1}{d} \frac{h}{|x^i|^d} \delta^{ab}\ , \quad \llangle T^{ai} \rrangle = 0\ ,\\
L000064	\llangle T^{ij} \rrangle &= \frac{h}{|x^i|^d} \left(\frac{p + 1}{d}\delta^{ij} - \frac{x^i x^j}{|x^i|^2}\right)\ ,
L000065	\end{split}
L000066	\end{equation}
L000067	up to a factor $h$, which characterizes the property of the defect~\cite{Billo:2016cpy}.
L000068	In this letter we are particularly interested in surface defects with $p=2$. In this case, there will be defect Weyl anomalies, similar to the Weyl anomalies in even-dimensional CFTs.

L000072	\begin{equation}

L000074	\end{equation}
L000075	with $R^\Sigma$ the intrinsic Ricci scalar of the defect submanifold $\Sigma$, $\Tilde{\Pi}_{ab}^{\mu}$ the traceless part of the second fundamental form, and $W_{abcd}$ the pullback of the bulk Weyl tensor. L000078	\end{equation}

L000080	\begin{equation}\label{eq-int-anomalyDef}

L000121	\textit{Supersymmetric R\'enyi entropy.}
L000122	R\'enyi entropy is a one parameter generalization of EE and provides information about the entanglement spectrum. It appears when we compute EE using the replica trick and returns to EE in the limit $n\to 1$,
L000123	\begin{equation}\label{eq-RE}
L000124	S_n \equiv \frac{1}{1-n} \log\mathrm{Tr}\rho^n = \frac{1}{1-n} \log\frac{Z_n}{Z^n}\ ,
L000125	\end{equation}
L000126	where $n$ is the R\'enyi index and $Z_n$ is the partition function on the $n$-replica space.

L000340	The $A_{N-1}$ $(2,0)$ SCFT is conjectured to be dual to M-theory on $\text{AdS}_7\times \mathbb{S}^4$ with $N$ units of 4-form flux on $\mathbb{S}^4$~\cite{Maldacena:1997re}. Furthermore, the holographic SRE of $A_{N-1}$ $(2,0)$ SCFT can be computed from 2-charge 7d topological black hole~\cite{Zhou:2015kaj},
L000341	\begin{equation}
L000342	\begin{split}
L000343	&\mathrm{d}s_7^2 = \frac{-f(r) \mathrm{d}t^2}{\left(H_1 H_2\right)^{4/5}} + \left(H_1 H_2\right)^{1/5} \left(\frac{\mathrm{d}r^2}{f(r)} + r^2 \mathrm{d}\Omega_{5,k}^2\right)\ ,\\
L000344	&f(r) = k - \frac{m}{r^4} + \frac{r^2}{L^2} H_1 H_2\ ,\quad H_i = 1 + \frac{q_i}{r^4}\ ,
L000345	\end{split}
L000346	\end{equation}
L000347	together with two scalars and two gauge fields,
L000348	\begin{equation}
L000349	X_i = \left(H_1 H_2\right)^{2/5}H_i^{-1}\ ,\quad A^i = \left(\sqrt{k} \left( H_i^{-1} - 1 \right) + \mu_i \right)\mathrm{d}t\ ,
L000350	\end{equation}
L000351	where we consider $k=-1$ and $m=0$.
L000352	Let us define a rescaled charge $\kappa_i = q_i/r_H^4$, then the black hole horizon can be expressed in terms of $\kappa_i$,
L000353	\begin{equation}\label{eq-BHgorizon}
L000354	r_H = \frac{L}{\sqrt{(1 + \kappa_1)(1 + \kappa_2)}}\ .
L000355	\end{equation}
L000356	The vanishing condition of $A^i$ at the horizon fixes the chemical potential
L000357	\begin{equation}\label{eq-chemicalP}
L000358	\mu_i = \frac{i}{\kappa_i^{-1} + 1}\ .
L000359	\end{equation}
L000360	The thermodynamics of this black hole can be solved straightforwardly, and here we focus on solving a probe M2-brane, which is the holographic dual of the surface operator in fundamental representation.
L000361	The expectation value of a half BPS surface defect $-\log\langle D\rangle_n$ can be computed from the M2-brane on-shell action, $I_{\text{M2}} = T_2 \int \mathrm{d}^3\sigma \sqrt{-\mathrm{det}\left[g_{\text{ind}}\right]}$. A recent work~\cite{Yuan:2023oni} has shown that it only depends on the horizon,
L000362	\begin{equation}\label{eq-IM2}
L000363	I_{\text{M2}} = -\pi n T_2 V_{\mathbb{H}^1} r_H^2\ .
L000364	\end{equation}
L000365	To match the chemical potentials of the boundary CFT, one should set
L000366	\begin{equation}\label{eq-mui-ri}
L000367	\mu_1 = i(\gamma - 1)\frac{r_1}{2}\ , \quad \mu_2 = i(\gamma - 1)\frac{r_2}{2}\ , \quad \text{with}\quad r_1 + r_2 = 1\ .
L000368	\end{equation}
L000369	From \eqref{eq-BHgorizon}, \eqref{eq-chemicalP} and \eqref{eq-mui-ri}, $r_H$ can be expressed in terms of $r_i$ and $\gamma$,
L000370	\begin{equation}\label{eq-rH2}
L000371	r_H^2 = L^2 \left( 1 - (1 - \gamma)\frac{r_1}{2} \right) \left( 1 - (1 - \gamma)\frac{r_2}{2} \right)\ .
L000372	\end{equation}
L000373	Using \eqref{eq-IM2} and \eqref{eq-rH2}, the defect contribution to holographic SRE is given by
L000374	\begin{equation}
L000375	\begin{split}
L000376	S_n &= \frac{\log\langle D\rangle_n - n \log\langle D\rangle_1}{1-n}\\
L000377	&= \pi T_2 V_{\mathbb{H}^1} L^2\big( r_1 r_2 (\gamma - 1) + 2 \big)/4\ .
L000378	\end{split}
L000379	\end{equation}
L000380	Given the holographic dictionary $N=L^3/(8\pi l_p^3)$ and $T_2 = 1/(4\pi^2l_p^3)$, it can be checked that when $n=1$, we have
L000381	$
L000382	I_{\text{M2}} = -4N\log\ell/\epsilon
L000383	$,
L000384	which agrees with the result in~\cite{Berenstein:1998ij, Drukker:2020dcz}. Moreover, we obtain the defect SRE in fundamental representation at the large $N$ limit,
L000385	\begin{equation}\label{eq-holographyFinal}
L000386	S_\gamma = N \big( r_1 r_2 (\gamma - 1) + 2 \big)\log\ell/\epsilon\ .
L000387	\end{equation}
L000388	
L000389	\textit{Discussions.} In this letter, we have proposed closed-form expressions for the surface defect contributions to the supersymmetric Rényi entropy and the supersymmetric Casimir energy in 6d (2,0) theories, formulated in terms of the defect central charges, $b$ and $d_2$. These formulas are supported by strong evidence and subjected to various consistency checks, further affirming their validity. Future directions include generalizing our approach to derive analogous formulas for co-dimension 2 defects, defects in 6d (1,0) SCFTs, and defects in 4d SCFTs. Additionally, it would be intriguing to explore bounds on central charges arising from these developments.

L000578	\subsection{Supersymmetric Entanglement entropy (SUSY EE) for Wilson loops in 4d}\label{appx-WL}
L000579	Here we show that for 4d $\mathcal{N} = 4$ SYM theory, the 1/2 BPS Wilson loop contribution to SUSY EE is
L000580	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WL-SEE}
L000581	S = \log\langle W \rangle - 6\pi^2 h_W\ ,
L000582	\end{equation}
L000583	where $h_W$ is the coefficient in the bulk stress tensor one-point function in the presence of a straight Wilson line in flat space, i.e.,
L000584	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WL-h-def}
L000585	\llangle T_{00} \rrangle \equiv \frac{\langle T_{00}W\rangle}{\langle W\rangle} = \frac{h_W}{r^4}\ ,
L000586	\end{equation}
L000587	with $r$ the distance between $T$ and the Wilson line. $h_W$ is the analogy to the $d_2$ central charge of surface defects. One can see that \eqref{eq-WL-SEE} shows a similar structure as the surface defect SUSY EE.
L000588	
L000589	To derive \eqref{eq-WL-SEE}, recall that the R\'enyi entropy of a spherical region in CFT$_d$ can be calculated from the Euclidean path integral on a branched $d$-sphere $\mathbb{S}^d_n$~\cite{Casini:2011kv, Klebanov:2011uf}
L000590	\begin{equation}
L000591	\mathrm{d}s^2 = n^2\sin^2 \theta \mathrm{d}\tau^2 + \mathrm{d}\theta^2 + \cos^2 \theta \mathrm{d}\Omega_{d - 2}^2\ .
L000592	\end{equation}
L000593	Here $\tau \in [0,2\pi)$, $\theta \in [0, \pi/2]$, and $\Omega_{d - 2}$ is the standard $(d - 2)$-dimensional round sphere. In the following we will focus on $d = 4$. In the consideration of supersymmetry, the branched four-sphere $\mathbb{S}^4_n$ can be replaced by the squashed four-sphere $\mathbb{S}^4_b$ given by the equation~\cite{Huang:2014pda}
L000594	\begin{equation}\label{eq-ellipsoid}
L000595	\frac{x_0^2}{r^2} + \frac{x_1^2 + x_2^2}{\ell^2} +\frac{x_3^2 + x_4^2}{\tilde{\ell}^2} = 1\ ,
L000596	\end{equation}
L000597	with $\ell = nr$, $\tilde{\ell} = r$, and the squashing parameter is defined as $b\equiv (\ell/\tilde{\ell})^{1/2} = \sqrt{n}$. The partition function on $\mathbb{S}^4_b$ for arbitrary $\mathcal{N} = 2$ gauge theories has been computed using localization technique~\cite{Hama:2012bg}, and with an insertion of a BPS Wilson loop, the localization procedure also goes through. For example, in $\mathcal{N} = 2$ SCFTs, the expectation value of the Wilson loop operator on $\mathbb{S}^4_b$ is given by~\cite{Hama:2012bg} (see also~\cite{Alday:2009fs, Fucito:2016jng})
L000598	\begin{equation}\label{eq-matrix-WL}
L000599	\langle W_b \rangle = \frac{\int \mathrm{d}a\,e^{-\frac{8\pi^2}{g^2} \mathrm{Tr}a^2} Z_{\text{1-loop}}(a,b)|Z_{\text{inst}}(a,b)|^2 \mathrm{Tr}e^{-2\pi b a}}{\int \mathrm{d}a\,e^{-\frac{8\pi^2}{g^2} \mathrm{Tr}a^2} Z_{\text{1-loop}}(a,b)|Z_{\text{inst}}(a,b)|^2}\ ,
L000600	\end{equation}
L000601	with the Wilson loop located in the $\{x_1,x_2\}$-plane~\footnote{There are two BPS Wilson loops on the $\mathbb{S}^4_b$ \eqref{eq-ellipsoid} and they transform into each other under $\ell \leftrightarrow \tilde{\ell}$. The expectation value of the second Wilson loop can be obtain by replacing $\mathrm{Tr}e^{-2\pi b a}$ by $\mathrm{Tr}e^{-2\pi b^{-1} a}$ in the matrix integral~\eqref{eq-matrix-WL}. }.
L000602	
L000603	For $\mathcal{N} = 4$ SYM theory, near $b = 1$, the localization result simplifies to
L000604	\begin{equation}
L000605	\langle W_b \rangle = \frac{\int \mathrm{d}a\,e^{-\frac{8\pi^2 N}{\lambda} \mathrm{Tr}a^2} \mathrm{Tr}e^{-2\pi b a}}{\int \mathrm{d}a\,e^{-\frac{8\pi^2 N}{\lambda} \mathrm{Tr}a^2}} + \mathcal{O}\left((b - 1)^2\right)\ ,
L000606	\end{equation}
L000607	which is manifestly a function of $b\sqrt{\lambda}$ after the rescaling $a = \sqrt{\lambda}\tilde{a}$~\cite{Fiol:2015spa},
L000608	\begin{equation}
L000609	\langle W_b \rangle = \frac{\int \mathrm{d}\tilde{a}\,e^{-8\pi^2 N \mathrm{Tr} \tilde{a}^2} \mathrm{Tr}e^{-2\pi b\sqrt{\lambda} \tilde{a}}}{\int \mathrm{d}\tilde{a}\,e^{-8\pi^2 N \mathrm{Tr} \tilde{a}^2}} + \cdots\ .
L000610	\end{equation}
L000611	
L000612	The Wilson loop contribution to SUSY EE is~\cite{Crossley:2014oea}
L000613	\begin{equation}
L000614	\begin{split}
L000615	S &= \left(1 - n\partial_n\right) \log\langle W_b \rangle |_{n \to 1}\\
L000616	&= \left(1 - \frac{1}{2}b\partial_b\right) \log\langle W_b \rangle |_{b \to 1}\ .
L000617	\end{split}
L000618	\end{equation}
L000619	Since $\langle W_b \rangle$ is a function of $b\sqrt{\lambda}$, there is a relation between its $b$-derivative and $\lambda$-derivative
L000620	\begin{equation}
L000621	\frac{1}{2} b\partial_b \log\langle W_b \rangle|_{b\to 1} = \lambda \partial_\lambda \log\langle W_b \rangle|_{b\to 1}\ .
L000622	\end{equation}
L000623	Using this relation, we obtain
L000624	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WL-susy-EE}
L000625	S = \left(1 -
L000626	\lambda\partial_\lambda\right) \log\langle W \rangle\ ,
L000627	\end{equation}
L000628	with $\langle W\rangle \equiv \langle W_{b = 1}\rangle$ the expectation value of 1/2 BPS Wilson loop on a round four-sphere.
L000629	
L000630	For $\mathcal{N} = 4$ SYM theory, the $\lambda$-derivative of $\log\langle W\rangle$ determines the bremsstrahlung function~\cite{Correa:2012at}
L000631	\begin{equation}\label{eq-B-lambda}
L000632	B = \frac{1}{2\pi^2} \lambda \partial_\lambda \log \langle W\rangle\ ,
L000633	\end{equation}
L000634	and in~\cite{Lewkowycz:2013laa} the authors find that for $\mathcal{N} = 4$ theories, $B$ is related to $h_W$ by~\footnote{The relation \eqref{eq-B-lambda} was first noticed in \cite{Fiol:2012sg}. }
L000635	\begin{equation}\label{eq-B-h}
L000636	B = 3 h_W\ .
L000637	\end{equation}
L000638	With \eqref{eq-WL-susy-EE}, \eqref{eq-B-lambda} and \eqref{eq-B-h}, the Wilson loop contribution to SUSY EE can be finally expressed as
L000639	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WL-SUSY-EE-final}
L000640	S = \left(1 - \lambda\partial_\lambda\right) \log\langle W \rangle = \log\langle W \rangle - 6\pi^2 h_W\ .
L000641	\end{equation}
L000642	In the strong coupling regime $ \log\langle W \rangle\approx\sqrt\lambda$, this is consistent with the holographic result presented in~\cite{Crossley:2014oea}. Note that \eqref{eq-WL-SUSY-EE-final} is different from the Wilson loop non-SUSY EE~\cite{Lewkowycz:2013laa}
L000643	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WL-nonSUSY-EE}
L000644	\tilde{S} = \log\langle W \rangle + \int \llangle T^\tau_\tau \rrangle = \log\langle W \rangle - 8\pi^2 h_W\ .
L000645	\end{equation}
L000646	
L000647	Here we give an explanation for the difference between the defect contribution to non-SUSY EE \eqref{eq-WL-nonSUSY-EE} and that for SUSY EE \eqref{eq-WL-SUSY-EE-final}. To illustrate, let us consider the calculation of \eqref{eq-WL-nonSUSY-EE} for free scalar theory. The second term proportional to $h_W$ comes from resolving the conical singularity at the entangling surface $\hat{\mit\Sigma}$ (the Wald term)~\cite{Lewkowycz:2013laa}. More precisely we smooth the tip of the cone and receive a $\delta$-function contribution to the Ricci scalar, which leads to the Wald term,
L000648	\begin{equation}\label{eq-WaldTerm}
L000649	S_{\text{Wald}} = -\frac{4\pi}{12}\int_{\hat{\mit\Sigma}}\mathrm{d}A \llangle\phi^2\rrangle\ .
L000650	\end{equation}
L000651	A similar story occurs in 6d free scalar theory with Wilson surface insertion~\cite{Yuan:2023oni}.
L000652	However, in the case of SUSY localization, we did not follow the same boundary condition. Instead we choose alternative boundary conditions compatible with SUSY. This is the reason why we get a different coefficient in front of $h_W$  in \eqref{eq-WL-nonSUSY-EE} and \eqref{eq-WL-SUSY-EE-final}.
